Instead of viewing jazz strictly as a performance product, this model provides emergency housing stipends, free hospital surgeries, disaster rebuilding, and pays musicians to bring music to Alzheimer's wards and Title I classrooms.
2. **Tuition-Free & Sliding-Scale Youth Development Centers:**
   - *Organizations:* **Seattle JazzED**, **New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Foundation (Heritage School of Music)**, **Philadelphia Clef Club**, **Jazz Outreach Initiative (JOI)**.
   - *Focus:* Removes the financial barrier to learning an instrument. They provide free instrument loan libraries, afterschool/weekend training, and explicit sliding-scale or 100% tuition-free models to ensure low-income and underrepresented youth can access high-level instruction.
3. **Public School System Supplementation & In-Classroom Integration:**
   - *Organizations:* **SFJAZZ**, **Jazz Aspen Snowmass (JAS In-Schools)**, **Herbie Hancock Institute of Jazz**.
   - *Focus:* Directly targets budget shortfalls in public education. They either replace eliminated music classes in rural/mountain corridors, integrate jazz into standard middle school history and humanities classes, or supply free nationwide curriculum materials.
4. **Civic Space Activation & Grassroots Cultural Preserves:**
   - *Organizations:* **Jazzmobile**, **Preservation Hall Foundation**, **Kuumbwa Jazz**, **The Carr Center**.
   - *Focus:* Reclaiming public space and cultural history. They bring free mobile concert stages into low-income public parks and housing complexes, preserve historic African American cultural unions and traditional New Orleans brass traditions, and operate community-staffed cultural hubs.

#### Most Common vs. Most Distinctive Approaches

- **Most Common Approaches:**
  - *In-School Masterclasses & Field Trips:* Nearly every organization brings musicians into schools or brings students into concert halls (e.g., SFJAZZ School Day Concerts, Preservation Hall's "Kids in the Hall", Jazzmobile's "Jazz in the First Person").
  - *Auditioned Youth Honors/Ensemble Academies:* Providing pre-professional training for teenagers with financial aid or free tuition (e.g., Clef Prep, LVYJO, Kuumbwa Honor Band, SFJAZZ All-Stars).
- **Most Distinctive Approaches:**
  - *Healthcare & Homelessness Intervention as Arts Preservation (Jazz Foundation of America):* Addressing social determinants of health (pro-bono hospital care, paying back rent) to keep musicians alive and sheltered.
  - *Gender Equity in Jazz Pedagogy (Seattle JazzED):* The "Femme Ellington Project" and gender-expansive jazz camps specifically dismantle the historical male dominance of jazz brass and rhythm sections.
  - *Peer-to-Peer Youth Diplomacy (Herbie Hancock Institute):* Using talented public high schoolers from one region to teach and inspire students in another state, teaching jazz as an exercise in democracy and conflict resolution.
  - *Mobile Stage Neighborhood Deployment (Jazzmobile):* Eliminating transportation and ticketing barriers by physically driving concerts into housing projects, public street corners, and neighborhood parks.
  - *Festival Reinvestment into Micro-Grants (New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Foundation):* Using commercial festival profits to fund micro-grants for local neighborhood artists and cultural small businesses.

- **Best For Designation:** **Best for Broader Community Outreach**

- **Why:** If you want your philanthropic support to prevent immediate human suffering, JFA is unmatched. - **Why:** They combine free, high-caliber year-round youth education (Heritage School of Music) with systemic community wealth-building. Education and Community Engagement

Music education is at the core of our mission to protect, preserve and perpetuate New Orleans musical traditions. Passing on the knowledge of this music to the next generation of New Orleans musicians is a primary focus of the Preservation Hall Foundation, as well as a personal focus and passion of many of the beloved musicians of Preservation Hall. 

Over the COVID-19 pandemic, we launched Preservation Hall Lessons, offering students and educators free digital learning materials and classroom-ready lesson plans on New Orleans music and culture. Today, we are thrilled to resume in-person education programming like Kids in the Hall at Preservation Hall, and in partnership with music organizations around the country – providing unforgettable, experiential settings for students, learning by playing, and experiencing lasting mentorship with musicians, tradition bearers, and teaching artists from the Preservation Hall collective of musicians.

Learning the New Orleans Way: 
Preservation Hall Lessons

The Preservation Hall Foundation has developed Preservation Hall Lessons: a free, online resource bank for teachers and music educators. The Lessons website includes a range of complete lesson plans for grades K-12, focusing on New Orleans style music, particularly traditional New Orleans Jazz and brass band music. The Lessons website is not just for regional use – it is now available for educators across the nation to help articulate the living art forms that exist in New Orleans on a national level, and ensure its inclusion in music education.

Brass Bandbook

The Preservation Hall Foundation Brass Bandbook is a free online resource for musicians and educators – complete with sheet music of 12 classic New Orleans tunes, like “Bourbon Street Parade and “Lil’ Liza Jane.” Complete with lyrics and historical context of the songs, this free sheet music is available for clarinet, trumpet, trombone, tuba, tenor sax, snare drum and bass drum at preshallfoundation.org/brassbandbook. 

ACCESS THE BRASS BANDBOOK→
Kids in the Hall

Classroom lessons come to life with the Preservation Hall Foundation's Kids in the Hall Field Trip program. In this one-hour field trip, students engage and listen to a Preservation Hall Band, as well as have an opportunity for a Q&A session with members of the Preservation Hall Collective. 

SIGN UP FOR A KIDS IN THE HALL FIELD TRIP →
Workshops, Masterclasses, and Open Soundchecks 

The Preservation Hall Foundation provides workshops, masterclasses, and open soundchecks to schools in the Greater New Orleans area and around the U.S., focusing on Brass Band and Traditional New Orleans Jazz. Open soundchecks are offered on 100% of the Preservation Hall Jazz Band's touring dates.  

To schedule a workshop or masterclass or to join us at an open soundcheck on any of Preservation Hall Jazz Band’s tour dates, email info@preshallfoundation.org.

Community Concerts

Community Concerts provides a range of free concerts in the Greater New Orleans area for communities limited in access to Preservation Hall by distance, economics, or other circumstances. These free concerts are performed by members of the Preservation Hall Collective and are designed for the whole family to attend. 

Stay tuned to our Facebook page for more details about upcoming concert performances.

Sousafund

In the wake of Ben Jaffe's Sousaphone being stolen, the Sousafund was established in 2018 to provide young bass and sousaphone students with high quality instruments. Students in Orleans and Jefferson Parish have received instruments and mentorship on upright bass or sousaphone.

JazzSprouts

JazzSprouts is a jazz education program designed for children 8 months to five years old. Jazz Jumpers

Students K-3 will explore the core elements of music through the lens of jazz. Through singing, movement, and hands-on instrument discovery, young musicians will learn about the rich history of artists, their iconic styles, and the cultural roots that shaped this uniquely American art form.

Foundations

Our Foundations class is for beginners in grades 4-8 with no previous music experience! Your budding musician will learn in with others in instrument groups built for individual learning and relationship building. HERITAGE SCHOOL OF MUSIC

THE DON “MOOSE” JAMISON HERITAGE SCHOOL OF MUSIC IS THE NEW ORLEANS JAZZ & HERITAGE FOUNDATION’S SIGNATURE EDUCATION PROGRAM.

Since 1990, the Don “Moose” Jamison Heritage School of Music, a free afterschool program, which serves nearly 300 students a week, from beginners aged 8 years old to advanced students aged 18 with in-depth music training, ensemble playing and music theory throughout the school year and summer school taught by some of the best musicians in New Orleans . 

Over the years, the program has experienced significant growth, particularly with the 2014 opening of the George and Joyce Wein Jazz & Heritage Center in New Orleans’ historic Tremé neighborhood, marking the school’s first-ever permanent home. This fully renovated facility boasts seven state-of-the-art classrooms equipped for music instruction, a 200-seat auditorium, and a recording studio, fostering an environment conducive to expanding the program and accommodating more students.

Today, the program also offers classes in audio and studio recording and vocal classes.  Students are accepted into the program at the beginning of school semesters.  The school’s commitment to nurturing young talent and promoting a deep appreciation for music underscores its valuable contribution to the community.

BECOME PART OF THE HERITAGE SCHOOL OF MUSIC FAMILY!

Our programs are free and open to students ages 8 to 18. No prior musical experience is required.

  2. *"Kids in the Hall" Field Trips & Open Soundchecks:* Brings local students on free, interactive field trips to Preservation Hall for live performance and musician Q&A; offers free open soundchecks and clinics in 100% of cities visited by the touring band.

  - *Attending:* Visible concert calendar for historic Preservation Hall and free community outreach events.
  - *Partnering:* Visible collaboration channels for visiting educators, schools, and cultural institutions.

#### 3. Seattle JazzED
- **Location:** Seattle, WA
- **3+ Concrete Ways It Serves the Community:**
  1. *Sliding-Scale Tuition & Free Instrument Loans:* Operates on a "choose-your-tuition-level" model with no-questions-asked 100% tuition waivers and free instrument loans, ensuring family income is never a barrier to musical training.
  2. *Equity-Centered Youth Ensembles:* Delivers structured instrumental training from ages 8 months through 12th grade (JazzSprouts, Foundations, Connections, Explorations, Summer Jazz Ambassadors) pairing musicianship with life mentorship.

  - *Partnering:* Visible school district partnership offerings (Black History Month assemblies, school clinics, teacher toolkits).

### Synthesis and Model Comparison

#### Grouping by Community Service Model

1. **Direct Social Safety Net & Musician Welfare:**
   - *Organizations:* **Jazz Foundation of America (JFA)**.
   - *Focus:* Treats jazz artists as vulnerable community cultural elders. Instead of viewing jazz strictly as a performance product, this model provides emergency housing stipends, free hospital surgeries, disaster rebuilding, and pays musicians to bring music to Alzheimer's wards and Title I classrooms.
2. **Tuition-Free & Sliding-Scale Youth Development Centers:**
   - *Organizations:* **Seattle JazzED**, **New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Foundation (Heritage School of Music)**, **Philadelphia Clef Club**, **Jazz Outreach Initiative (JOI)**.
   - *Focus:* Removes the financial barrier to learning an instrument. They provide free instrument loan libraries, afterschool/weekend training, and explicit sliding-scale or 100% tuition-free models to ensure low-income and underrepresented youth can access high-level instruction.
3. **Public School System Supplementation & In-Classroom Integration:**
   - *Organizations:* **SFJAZZ**, **Jazz Aspen Snowmass (JAS In-Schools)**, **Herbie Hancock Institute of Jazz**.
   - *Focus:* Directly targets budget shortfalls in public education. They either replace eliminated music classes in rural/mountain corridors, integrate jazz into standard middle school history and humanities classes, or supply free nationwide curriculum materials.
4. **Civic Space Activation & Grassroots Cultural Preserves:**
   - *Organizations:* **Jazzmobile**, **Preservation Hall Foundation**, **Kuumbwa Jazz**, **The Carr Center**.
   - *Focus:* Reclaiming public space and cultural history. They bring free mobile concert stages into low-income public parks and housing complexes, preserve historic African American cultural unions and traditional New Orleans brass traditions, and operate community-staffed cultural hubs.

#### Most Common vs. Most Distinctive Approaches

- **Most Common Approaches:**
  - *In-School Masterclasses & Field Trips:* Nearly every organization brings musicians into schools or brings students into concert halls (e.g., SFJAZZ School Day Concerts, Preservation Hall's "Kids in the Hall", Jazzmobile's "Jazz in the First Person").
  - *Auditioned Youth Honors/Ensemble Academies:* Providing pre-professional training for teenagers with financial aid or free tuition (e.g., Clef Prep, LVYJO, Kuumbwa Honor Band, SFJAZZ All-Stars).
- **Most Distinctive Approaches:**
  - *Healthcare & Homelessness Intervention as Arts Preservation (Jazz Foundation of America):* Addressing social determinants of health (pro-bono hospital care, paying back rent) to keep musicians alive and sheltered.
  - *Gender Equity in Jazz Pedagogy (Seattle JazzED):* The "Femme Ellington Project" and gender-expansive jazz camps specifically dismantle the historical male dominance of jazz brass and rhythm sections.
  - *Peer-to-Peer Youth Diplomacy (Herbie Hancock Institute):* Using talented public high schoolers from one region to teach and inspire students in another state, teaching jazz as an exercise in democracy and conflict resolution.
  - *Mobile Stage Neighborhood Deployment (Jazzmobile):* Eliminating transportation and ticketing barriers by physically driving concerts into housing projects, public street corners, and neighborhood parks.
  - *Festival Reinvestment into Micro-Grants (New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Foundation):* Using commercial festival profits to fund micro-grants for local neighborhood artists and cultural small businesses.

For an outsider looking to get involved through hands-on volunteering, impactful donations, or community-serving partnerships, these are the 5 strongest organizations:

#### 1. Seattle JazzED (Ranked #1 — Overall Hands-on Youth Impact)
- **Why:** They have created the most intentional, barrier-free community music school model in the country. Their commitment to 100% tuition sliding scales (no proof of income required), free instrument checkouts, and programs targeting historically underrepresented young women and non-binary youth makes every dollar and hour directly transform a young person's daily life.

- **Why:** Unlike many established jazz institutions that restrict public participation to passive financial donations, JOI built a structured, welcoming community volunteer wing (**The JOI Jazz Alliance**). A community member can directly apply on their site to support Title 1 school clinics, youth orchestra logistics, and community jams, making it ideal for someone who wants to roll up their sleeves immediately.
- **Best For Designation:** **Best for Volunteering**

#### 3. Jazzmobile (Ranked #3 — Purest Broader Community Outreach)
- **Why:** For 60 years, Jazzmobile has maintained the purest neighborhood-level outreach model in urban America. By mounting concerts on mobile stages in public parks, senior centers, and public housing courtyards where people gather, they eliminate economic, cultural, and geographic gatekeeping, making world-class music a free public utility.
- **Best For Designation:** **Best for Broader Community Outreach**

- **Why:** If you want your philanthropic support to prevent immediate human suffering, JFA is unmatched. #### 5. New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Foundation (Ranked #5 — Best Systemic Community Investment Model)
- **Why:** They combine free, high-caliber year-round youth education (Heritage School of Music) with systemic community wealth-building. Because they operate active year-round volunteer programs and distribute direct grants to local artists and schools, they represent the gold standard for how cultural assets can be reinvested into a city's social fabric.
